opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate them, because they're doing different work, even though in practice they compound.

Scaling is the baseline trend: more compute, better algorithms, more data. Each order of magnitude gets you a smarter model in a raw sense: better world knowledge, better intuitions, fewer dumb mistakes. If you just look at the curve from GPT-2 to GPT-4, that's mostly what drove it. You went from something like a preschooler to something like a smart high schooler, and nobody had to invent a fundamentally new paradigm along the way.

But there's a second thing I call "unhobbling." The models are really smart in some ways, yet we've been using them in an incredibly handicapped way. Right now, when you ask a chatbot something, it's basically forced to answer System 1, off the top of its head. Imagine asking a person to solve a hard math problem or write a complex piece of software, but they have to just start talking immediately and can't stop to think, can't backtrack, can't check their work, can't open a scratchpad. Even a very smart person would look pretty mediocre under those constraints.

So teaching models System 2 reasoning is about unlocking the ability to think for a long time. Instead of a few hundred tokens, the model can spend thousands or millions of tokens working through a problem, notice errors, try another approach, plan, and execute over hours or days. That's what turns a chatbot into something more like an agent, or a drop-in remote worker.

The way I'd distinguish them: scaling raises the ceiling of raw intelligence per token, and unhobbling lets you actually use that intelligence over a long horizon. And the key bet is that the unhobbling part may be relatively cheap. You might not need to train a brand-new giant model. Plausibly the models already have most of the raw capability, and what's missing is learning to error-correct, to stay on track, and to use test-time compute productively. Some RL, some clever training, a little bit of the right data on long-horizon tasks, and you get a huge effective jump.

If both work out, they multiply. You get another couple orders of magnitude of effective compute from scaling, and on top of that you unlock long-horizon reasoning. That's why I think the jump over the next few years could be as big as GPT-2 to GPT-4, or bigger, qualitatively. It wouldn't just be a smarter chatbot. It would be something that can actually go off and do the work.

The honest uncertainty is whether the System 2 piece turns out to be easy or hard. That's the crux. If it's harder than I expect, you could hit a period where models are very smart but still kind of stuck being chatbots. I'd say the evidence is pointing toward it being tractable.

r001.rationale: It suggests some RL, clever training, and a little data, but does not say the added learning consists of a small set of token patterns.

r002.rationale: It says scaling improves raw intelligence, world knowledge, intuitions, and fewer mistakes, while describing current chatbot responses as System 1 and off the top of their head.

r003.rationale: It says System 2 training could let models work through thousands or millions of tokens over long horizons.

r004.rationale: It says models may already have most raw capability and that learning to use test-time compute productively could unlock a huge effective jump.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as two pretty distinct axes, and part of why I'm fairly confident about where things are going is that you get progress on both simultaneously.

The first axis is just raw scaling: more compute, more data, bigger models. And the thing to appreciate about scaling is that it's been remarkably regular. You go from GPT-2 to GPT-4, that's roughly a preschooler to a smart high schooler in four years. The scaling laws held, and if you count the orders of magnitude of effective compute coming over the next few years, from physical compute plus algorithmic efficiencies, you get another jump of similar size. That gets you a model that's just raw-smarter, better at pattern-matching, more knowledgeable, more fluent.

But I think scaling alone doesn't get you an agent. Right now, what we've got is something that's incredibly smart in the moment, but it's basically operating like you would if you had to answer every question off the top of your head, with no scratchpad, in a few seconds. It's System 1. Even GPT-4 is like a brilliant person who's only allowed to blurt out the first thing that comes to mind.

The second axis is what I'd call "unhobbling." The models have these very obvious limitations that aren't about intelligence per se. They can't think for very long. They can't go back and check their work, try a different approach when they're stuck, plan over a horizon of days or weeks. A human doing a hard problem will think for hours, run experiments, iterate. The model, so far, gets a few hundred tokens of chain of thought and that's it.

Teaching models System 2 reasoning is about fixing that. And the key thing is that it's an algorithmic problem, not a scale problem. Chain of thought was a tiny unlock, basically free, and it was worth a lot of effective compute. RLHF turned a base model that was useless to most people into something you'd actually want to talk to. Those weren't scaling gains, they were unhobbling gains. And I think the big remaining one is exactly this: can the model learn to use test-time compute productively? Can it think for the equivalent of a workday or a work-month rather than a few minutes?

Why does that matter for agents specifically? Because an agent is defined by the long horizon. It has to hold a goal, decompose it, execute steps, notice when something's gone wrong, recover. All of that is System 2. You can have an arbitrarily sharp model that still can't do a multi-week engineering task if it can't reason over long horizons and correct itself.

So the way I'd put the distinction is: scaling makes the underlying "brain" smarter, and unhobbling lets that brain actually do things. And the reason I'm bullish is that I don't think these are independent bets where you need one or the other to pay off. You're getting the scaling almost mechanically because of the compute buildout. And the System 2 piece is a problem where you have a very clear target, a lot of smart people working on it, and lots of early signals that it's tractable. If you get both, which I think is the default, that's when you go from a chatbot to something that looks like a drop-in remote worker. And that's when it starts to feel very different.

r002.rationale: It describes scaling as making the model “raw-smarter” and better at pattern-matching, knowledge, and fluency, consistent with improving its System 1-like, in-the-moment capabilities.

r003.rationale: It discusses thinking for a workday or work-month, but does not claim coherent reasoning over millions of tokens.

r004.rationale: It identifies learning to use test-time compute productively as the key System 2 goal and says that this can let the model reason over much longer horizons.

astra-6.text:
I think those are complementary rather than competing paths. Scaling gives you a better base model: it knows more, it can make more useful connections, and it’s more capable of figuring things out. But there’s a separate question of how you use that capability. Do you ask it to produce an answer immediately, or can it spend time working through a problem, checking its work, and trying a different approach when it gets stuck?

That’s the distinction I’d draw with System 2 reasoning. A human doing a difficult task doesn’t just have one thought and announce the answer. You might spend an hour writing things down, testing an idea, realizing it doesn’t work, and backing up. We want models to be able to use additional computation in that productive way.

But simply telling a model to think for longer isn’t enough. If it can’t distinguish progress from a dead end, you may just get a longer chain of mistakes. You need to train the process so that additional time actually improves the result.

For agents, that matters enormously. Answering a question is one thing; pursuing a goal through many steps, noticing errors, and recovering from them is another. Scaling helps supply the underlying capability, while learning to deliberate and correct course helps turn that capability into reliable action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training deliberation but does not say it may require learning only a small set of additional token patterns.

r002.rationale: It says scaling improves the base model’s knowledge and capability, but does not characterize this as improving System 1-like autopilot abilities.

r003.rationale: It describes spending time on problems without claiming coherent thought over millions of tokens.

r004.rationale: It says additional computation can improve results when the process is trained, but does not claim System 2 unlocks latent capability from additional test-time compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are complementary rather than competing paths. Scaling gives you a smarter base model: it knows more, recognizes more patterns, and can handle harder problems. But that doesn’t automatically mean it can work autonomously for hours, check its own work, or recover when something goes wrong.

With System 2 reasoning, the idea is to let the model spend more computation on a problem. Instead of producing an answer immediately, it can break the problem into steps, try an approach, notice that it failed, and try something else. For an agent, that’s very important, because accomplishing a task involves a whole sequence of decisions, not just one good response.

But you can’t completely separate that from scaling. A model needs enough underlying capability for its attempts at reasoning and self-correction to be useful. And then you need training that teaches it how to use that capability over longer stretches. So the question is both how smart the model is and how effectively it can turn that intelligence into sustained work.
